                    ### Question
                    A 62-year-old man with gastroesophageal reflux disease and osteoarthritis is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-hour history of severe, stabbing epigastric pain. For the last 6 months, he has had progressively worsening right knee pain, for which he takes ibuprofen several times a day. He has smoked half a pack of cigarettes daily for 25 years. The lungs are clear to auscultation. An ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ST-segment elevations or depressions. This patient is most likely to have referred pain in which of the following locations?

                    ### Options

opb. Left shoulder
opc. Umbilicus

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with severe, stabbing epigastric pain, which raises the possibility of gastrointestinal issues, particularly given his history of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). GERD can cause referred pain, commonly to the right scapula due to the shared nerve pathways (phrenic nerve). The ECG shows sinus tachycardia, which could suggest cardiac issues, but the absence of ST-segment changes makes acute myocardial ischemia less likely. Referred pain to the left shoulder is also a consideration in cardiac conditions, but the primary symptom is epigastric pain, which aligns more with GERD-related referred pain. The other options, such as umbilicus, left jaw, and right groin, are less commonly associated with epigastric pain. Therefore, the most likely site of referred pain in this case is the right scapula.
